summary.text: Cramer's rule is an explicit formula for solving a system of linear equations with as many equations as unknowns, valid whenever the system has a unique solution.
It writes the solution using determinants of the coefficient matrix and of matrices where one column is replaced by the right-hand sides.
It is named after Gabriel Cramer, who published it in 1750, though Colin Maclaurin published special cases in 1748.

facts.label: Published
facts.value: Gabriel Cramer, 1750, for any number of unknowns

facts.label: Earlier cases
facts.value: Colin Maclaurin published special cases in 1748

facts.label: Number system
facts.value: Works over any field, not just real numbers

facts.label: Requirement
facts.value: The coefficient determinant must be nonzero

facts.label: Geometry
facts.value: A determinant of n vectors gives a parallelepiped's volume

items.prompt: A system has three equations but four unknowns. Can Cramer's rule be used directly?

options.label: No, it needs as many equations as unknowns
Yes, whenever any solution exists
Yes, if all coefficients are whole numbers
No, it only works with two unknowns

items.explain: The rule applies to systems with as many equations as unknowns.

items.prompt: You compute the coefficient determinant and it comes out zero. What does that tell you?

options.label: The system has exactly one solution
All the unknowns are zero
The rule does not apply to this system
The solution is zero for every unknown

items.explain: Cramer's rule applies to the case where the coefficient determinant is nonzero.

items.prompt: To find the second unknown with Cramer's rule, how do you build the matrix for its numerator?

options.label: Delete the second row
Replace the second column with the right-hand sides
Replace the second row with the right-hand sides
Swap the first and second columns

items.explain: The numerator matrix replaces one column of the coefficient matrix by the column of right-hand sides.

items.prompt: A 2×2 system has coefficient determinant zero but nonzero numerator determinants. What is it?

options.label: Solved by all unknowns being zero
Indeterminate, with infinitely many
Uniquely solvable
Inconsistent, with no solutions

items.explain: In the 2×2 case, a zero coefficient determinant with nonzero numerators means the system is inconsistent.

items.prompt: Someone says Cramer's rule only works when the coefficients are real numbers. Is that right?

options.label: No, it holds in any field
Yes, real numbers only
Yes, but whole numbers too
No, but only for rational numbers

items.explain: The rule holds for coefficients and unknowns in any field, not just the real numbers.

items.prompt: Geometrically, what does the determinant of n vectors of length n give?

options.label: The angle between the first two
The sum of their lengths
The volume of the parallelepiped they determine
The number of solutions

items.explain: The determinant of n vectors of length n gives the volume of the parallelepiped they determine.
